articles.author: Jesse Hassenger
articles.content: In the sixth episode of the short 29th season, the citizens of ‘South America’ reckon with corruption, AI and the unifying power of a certain video game South Park’s 29th season may not have been long but it’s fair to say it braided a skilful running storyline. Over the season’s first five episodes, it seemed increasingly likely that the sixth and final instalment would centre on the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI – and it did. The episode, written by Trey Parker, opened on the empty streets of “South America” where everyone from toddlers to seniors was happily playing GTA VI on their couches. But when a series of power outages interferes with both the game and players’ ability to save their progress, the streets are soon flooded with angry citizens brandishing their PlayStations. Though public officials won’t say so, it becomes clear that they’ve acquiesced to the billionaires who have insisted they need power-sucking datacentres to “do AI”, as the show amusingly words it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alex Needham
articles.content: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.content: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Images As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports . If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation , albeit without giving any potential launch window. These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow. Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems. Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial , it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”. What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite? A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”. A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to: place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere. Read more: Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it A nuclear ‘aurora’ No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth. One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “ aurora ”. One eyewitness , then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”. The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime. The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities. Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage . The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu. Capnez/Wikimedia What happens in space is a threat on Earth Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit. These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “ space citizens ”. Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”. During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance. Mitigating the threat through verification So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space? As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition. The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument. Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report , they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”. The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections. In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch. As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise , we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968. The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations. The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk. In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space. Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too. Art Cotterell's postdoctoral fellowship is co-funded by the UNSW Nuclear Innovation Centre and UNSW Law & Justice. He is affiliated with the Australasian Centre for Space Governance.

articles.content: The guitarist was absolutely integral to Duran Duran’s success, and not merely because he was by far the band’s most straightforwardly talented musician Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65 Andy Taylor – a life in pictures It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music. Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose. Continue reading...

articles.content: Deagreez/Getty Images Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others. We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content. Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover it had been generated by AI. The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognise it at all. The synthetic trap People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy, are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real. However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognising when they’ve been misled. In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real. Therefore, many Australians may not recognise when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information. Trust in AI is low While AI use has grown rapidly, many are sceptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact on society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform. Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?”, only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%). Our survey also shows people are particularly distrusting of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively. In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society. How do people verify content? Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI generated. When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news. Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinise the content itself and rely on their own judgement. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing. Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups. Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information. People want strong safeguards Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it. Most importantly, they want protections to ensure the accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform. They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates. This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government. First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labelling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from. Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognise synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices. We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives. Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. articles.description: Deagreez/Getty Images Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others. We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content. Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover it had been generated by AI. The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognise it at all. The synthetic trap People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy, are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real. However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognising when they’ve been misled. In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real. Therefore, many Australians may not recognise when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information. Trust in AI is low While AI use has grown rapidly, many are sceptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact on society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform. Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?”, only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%). Our survey also shows people are particularly distrusting of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively. In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society. How do people verify content? Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI generated. When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news. Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinise the content itself and rely on their own judgement. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing. Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information. People want strong safeguards Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it. Most importantly, they want protections to ensure the accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform. They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates. This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government. First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labelling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from. Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognise synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices. We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives. Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. articles.content: It started as a joke, but Tightarses of Melbourne has grown into a thriving community. Accompanied by its founder Lisa Lorenz, Guardian Australia tests how much bang you can get for $50 Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email In 2022 Lisa Lorenz was working in music promotion when the overpriced culinary options and long lines at Melbourne’s Moomba festival led her and her partner to Clocks, the much passed over pokies-cum-tavern at Flinders Street station. The cocktails were $10 and the vibe on the bustling terrace was surprisingly satisfying. “It’s the kind of place most people would never think to go, but we were having such a great afternoon, chatting to people and watching the world go by,” she tells me. As the drinks continued to flow the pair were compelled to spread the good word. They took a few “intentionally terrible photos”, created an Instagram page and Tightarses of Melbourne, a guide to the city’s scrimpiest food and drink specials, was born. Continue reading...

articles.content: Fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resource on which their businesses depend Raising more tax revenue from our gas industry is the closest thing you will find to a public policy no-brainer . There are numerous calls for the government to return the budget to surplus quickly, in contrast to the current forecasts of continuing budget deficits well into the future. Those calling for a return to surplus generally want large net expenditure cuts, which are difficult given the pressure to spend more on an ageing population and on defence, just to name two areas. I believe this will only succeed if, in addition to better control of expenditure, there is focus on the revenue side. In this context, by far the easiest step is to collect more tax from our gas industry . Continue reading...

articles.content: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Morning Mail here , and finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter . Morning everyone. More fossil fuels, more punishment and less tax. These are just a few of the things Victorians may be in for if they vote for a Coalition government on Saturday. The fossil fuel question lurks behind another top story this morning, which reveals the world has experienced six consecutive days of dangerously high temperatures for the first time. Also, students speak against oral assessments, we examine the pain of youth unemployment, and a Big Bash batter falls foul of a timing rule. Timed out | Melbourne Renegades all-rounder Deandra Dottin became the first victim of a new rule in the Women’s Big Bash League last night when she failed to reach the crease in time to begin her innings, leaving Brisbane Heat’s Sarah ⁠Glenn to bowl at – and hit – her unattended stumps. articles.content: NASA/JPL/NGA , CC BY-SA The 600-kilometre Alpine Fault is one of New Zealand’s largest earthquake hazards. In our new study , we used fibre optic cables to map the fault in unprecedented detail to show how future earthquakes might unfold. The Alpine Fault runs the length of the Southern Alps and defines the boundary between the Australian and Pacific tectonic plates. It has been the focus of extensive geological , seismological and drilling investigations in recent years because it produces very large (magnitude 7-8) earthquakes about every 300 years. With the most recent earthquake in 1717, scientists estimate there’s a 75% chance of a large one in the next 50 years , with high odds it will be larger than magnitude 8. In anticipation of that event, several research groups are working hard to understand how the Alpine Fault is being loaded prior to its next rupture and how its geometry and physical characteristics may affect an earthquake’s propagation and the resulting ground shaking. Our focus is on determining the fault’s geometry and internal structure at scales much finer than can be studied using conventional seismometers, which are usually spaced tens of kilometres apart. Instead we used a standard telecommunications cable to reveal the fault’s internal detail. Our study shows the fault is not a single clean crack but rather a band of damaged rock about 200 metres wide. The Alpine Fault is a wide band of damaged rock, with narrower zones where it likely slipped. Author provided , CC BY-SA Within it, we found six much narrower zones of more intensely crushed and sheared rock. We call these “cores” and think the most prominent core is where the fault slipped during recent large earthquakes. This matters because an earthquake’s size depends mainly on how much of the fault breaks. Understanding the fault’s structure helps us work out how much could break at once, and how large the next big earthquake might be. Lighting up the Alpine Fault We send pulses of laser light down an optical fibre in a cable installed by telecommunications company Chorus near Haast. This turns the cable into a long line of sensitive earthquake sensors. We used a technique called distributed acoustic sensing ( DAS ). This records microscopic vibrations of the cable by measuring how each laser pulse is scattered by atomic-scale imperfections in the glass fibre. Our measurements show seismic waves produced by nearby small earthquakes travel along the fault as distinctive energy pulses known as fault zone guided waves. The propagation of these waves along a fault is similar to how light travels along an optical fibre. The fault zone guided waves we have recorded reveal the discrete cores, only about 10 metres wide, within the 200-metre zone of damaged rock. A fibre-optic cable near Haast recorded earthquake waves guided by the Alpine Fault, revealing several narrow fault cores within a wider zone of damaged rock. The circle size shows earthquake magnitude. Green circles mark earthquakes with clear guided waves, and orange circles mark those with less distinct guided waves. Voon Hui Lai , CC BY-SA Our observations suggest one of the cores extends continuously for about 180 kilometres along the Alpine Fault, from Martins Bay at least as far as Karangarua. While the fault bends and kinks at the surface, our new measurements imply that, deep underground, its main slip zone appears to be largely continuous. Whether slip occurs on a single smooth surface, as our observations suggest, or on separate, discontinuous fault structures likely influences the extent and direction of rupture, and hence the ground shaking it produces. Significantly, the most prominent core extends across a distinct change in the Alpine Fault’s geometry near Martyr River. There the dipping geometry characteristic of the fault along much of the West Coast alters to a steeper, almost vertical geometry extending towards Milford Sound. Earlier research suggests many past earthquakes have started or stopped near Martyr River. Determining which factors control the start and end of an earthquake along the Alpine Fault, including whether slip occurs on a single, continuous surface or jumps between separate faults, is crucial to understanding the likely extent of future ruptures. This in turn determines the earthquake’s overall magnitude and resulting ground shaking. Another recent study used grooves scratched onto a fault plane, known as “slickenlines”, to show the Alpine Fault ruptured from south to north in the last large earthquake in 1717. If a future Alpine Fault quake were to rupture in a south to north direction, it would cause higher-intensity shaking in the populated regions of Canterbury, Marlborough, Tasman and the northern West Coast. In contrast, a north to south rupture would propagate towards Fiordland, where fewer people live. The DAS measurements we made at Haast enable us to describe the fine-scale internal structure of the Alpine Fault at depths relevant to earthquake nucleation and propagation. Together with other studies, we are building a clearer picture of how different sections of the fault are connected in locations where large earthquakes appear to preferentially start or stop. Our observations will provide vital information for future models of rupture progression and the radiation of seismic energy that causes ground shaking. Understanding this will help New Zealand prepare for the hazard and the impacts of future Alpine Fault earthquakes. John Townend has received funding from the Catalyst and Marsden funds, both administered by the Royal Society Te Apārangi; the Natural Hazards Commission Toka Tū Ake; and the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment. He serves as chair of the publications committee of the Seismological Society of America. Meghan S. Miller receives funding from the Australian Research Council and from National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) in her role as program director of AuScope Earth Imaging. Voon Hui Lai receives funding from Singapore Ministry of Education (MOE) AcRF Tier 3b project “Investigating Volcano and Earthquake Science and Technology (InVEST)”.

Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. articles.content: New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’ Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal? If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Fisher in Istanbul
articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.content: The state attorney general says she would ‘not hesitate to enforce’ the five-year ban signed by Governor Kathy Hochul The New York governor, Kathy Hochul , signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. articles.content: Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. In this constantly changing world of global disruptions, uncertainties and risks, with social, political and economic disaffection seemingly on the rise everywhere, it’s genuinely heartening to know that some things never change . ‘Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose’, as the late, great French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr famously said, something that I’m sure Big Dunc is well aware of” – Noble Francis. May I be the 1,092nd correspondent to demand a review of the Letter o’ the Day award for Monday – and it be awarded to Declan Hackett for his letter foretelling the rescinding of the red card given to Lenny Yoro on Sunday? Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Beasley
articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.content: Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi . Russo is perhaps best known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, which had an aesthetic inspired by 60s and 70s men’s magazines; The Fox has a similarly thick retro texture. I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Martin Pegan
articles.content: One or perhaps more spots are up for grabs ahead of the summer series against New Zealand. We assess the leading batters’ chances of being picked in the XI Australia’s cricketers would be within their rights to be counting down the days until attention turns to the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand in Perth. As the sandpapergate scandal overshadows a pair of white-ball series against arch-rivals England, batters around the country have been pressing their claims for a place in Australia’s XI when the Chappell-Hadlee Trophy series begins on 9 December. A vacancy has already opened at the top of the order after selectors took the unusual step to confirm earlier this month that Marnus Labuschagne had been dropped from the squad for the four-Test series. The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. Continue reading...

articles.content: After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history. articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
articles.content: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jack Seale
articles.content: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Downie
articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.author: Phil Walker
articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart. More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare? Continue reading...

articles.content: Apple’s tone-deaf Karate Kid knock-off feels like a Maga-approved after-school special It’s hard to avoid the reports that boys and young men are in trouble . Across the US and UK, they’re outpaced by girls on reading tests, are more likely to have behavioral difficulties and exposed to impossible body image standards by the manosphere. You might think that all of this would make you think extra carefully about a film that centers on a 13-year-old boy. Not in the case of Way of the Warrior Kid, a cliche-ridden celebration of machismo and the military that greets the current climate with a shrug. At times, I had to remind myself that I wasn’t watching a Maga-funded after-school special. Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Hattenstone
articles.content: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.author: Flora Willson
articles.content: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no other. Continue reading...

articles.content: Vivienne Foroughirad/Texas A&M/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project In the turquoise waters of Western Australia’s Shark Bay lives a large resident population of dolphins. Some of these marine mammals are 54 years old, others just infants. But no matter their age, they live highly social lives. Researchers have studied these dolphins for decades . Forty years on, our extensive dataset reveals crucial insights into how these animals socialise throughout their lives – and how their social choices affect their health and fitness. In our new study , published in PLOS Biology, we analysed nearly 40 years of data on over 450 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops aduncus ) from Shark Bay. We found that as dolphins navigate their social world, they develop unique personalities and social preferences, and individuals who are consistent about these preferences may live longer. Sociality is a spectrum Dolphins’ social lives mirror our own in remarkable ways. As they navigate their blue world, dolphins move in and out of social groups, constantly making decisions about who to spend time with and who to avoid, depending on the task at hand. Much like humans, dolphins vary markedly in how social they are. Research shows some are more cliquish, while others are true social butterflies, embedded in large and complex social networks These differences matter. Just as in humans and many other species, the way dolphins navigate their social lives can shape their survival, longevity and reproductive success. For example, strong social connections promote resilience, while social isolation can increase mortality risk . Such patterns are not set in stone either. In many species , including humans, social behaviour is shaped as we age. In humans, social networks often become smaller, with older adults becoming more selective, investing their time and energy in a smaller number of meaningful relationships. But what happens as dolphins age? Previous research on dolphins has shown us that extended maternal care in older dolphin mothers is evidence of reproductive senescence – similar to menopause in humans. This raises an intriguing question: do dolphins also show other patterns of ageing like our own? Drone footage of six individuals who reside in nearshore habitat off the coast of Monkey Mia, Shark Bay. In front from left to right are Risotto (24) and her calf, Linguini (2), who is in a nursing position; Whoops (27), and Wags (6). Behind them are two more individuals; Risotto’s previous calf Arancini (6), and Jungle (8). Diana Alvarado/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project , CC BY Social ageing can be measured in multiple ways As we age, we develop personalities, build and lose relationships, and create our unique social environment which changes with each passing year. This process of social change as we grow is called social ageing . Most studies of social ageing have examined how individuals change over time by collecting many measurements, then finding their average. This can be useful for dolphins that have only a few close companions. But for those who frequently join groups large and small, an average tells us very little. We can instead turn to another measurement: predictability . This describes the spread of an individual’s data. Those dolphins who consistently spend time with the same number of other dolphins are very predictable. Those who flit between groups of many sizes are much less predictable. Predictability is difficult to measure because it requires a single individual be measured dozens, even hundreds, of times. Luckily, with 40 years of data on over 450 dolphins, research can go beneath the surface to study not only how individuals change in sociability with age on average, but how predictable they are, and if predictability can change, too. Being consistent is key For our new study, we examined the effects of sex, age, and individual personality on group size (a measure of sociability) throughout the population of dolphins at Shark Bay. We discovered several key points. First, dolphins follow a pattern very similar to humans and other long-lived species: they increase their average group size with age, to a point. After that point, which is unique to each individual, those average group sizes begin to decrease. Second, regardless of what their average group size is, individuals become more predictable with age. Third, males had a higher average group size and higher predictability than females. Finally, individuals who continued to increase their group size average and predictability most with age lived longer. Social stability can being a sustaining force Our research into dolphins’ social lives suggests that developing a strong and stable social environment can buffer many of the effects of ageing and enhance lifespan. Studying dolphins’ social traits reveals that it’s not only average behaviour which shapes fitness outcomes, but individual predictability. To truly understand how ageing shapes us, we must look beyond the average to see how the predictability of our social decisions can affect us as we navigate our world. This study reinforces the importance of maintaining consistent social relationships throughout the ageing process. In the case of the Shark Bay dolphins, it’s not only about how large one’s social circle is; rather, it’s about the social circle staying roughly the same size and type over size. And this holds an important lesson for us, because the trends we find in dolphins closely parallel the sort of patterns we see in human social behaviour as well. Kelley Meehan has received direct research funding from the Holsworth Wildlife Research Endowment, the Australian Research Training Program Scholarship, and the SQuID Fellowship. This project has received grant funding from the National Science Foundation and the US Office of Naval Research, as well as material support from the Royal Automobile Club Monkey Mia Resort. Celine Frere receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the US National Science Foundation. Janet Mann receives funding from The National Science Foundation for the long-term Shark Bay dolphin research.

articles.author: Anna Spargo-Ryan
articles.content: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her. The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done. Continue reading...

articles.content: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg – who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024 – would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut. To “buy a seat” on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark . There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a home-grown astronaut to space would yield potential benefits to industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be a powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space. However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it’s costly. As we’re in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine , it’s crucial to properly analyse some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal. What counts as an Australian astronaut? The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately. The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space . But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn’t been given the label of the first “female Australian astronaut”. The federal government hasn’t signalled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal “ reckless ”. These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then Minister for Science, Barry Jones, noted it wasn’t a high priority . Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in. The cost would be substantial We don’t know if Australians would support spending $100m on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut programme, but respondents were not given a cost. Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs , public support decreases. When asked in 2023 , more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canned. Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently the Australian Space Agency’s funding is $21.7m over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund a decade for the agency. Put another way, $100m is half of the total government investment in space or space adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occurs at universities, in government agencies, and in private industry; many organisations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply. Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There’s no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming . An astronaut can’t meet all these needs, and we don’t know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn’t have a whole of government space policy and an astronaut is not a space program. The suggestion that Australia’s growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space? ESA has a geographic return policy which sees member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state, and not looking to be. The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it’s difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based. What about inspiration? Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg’s selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country. However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM. The selection process was not nationally competitive and there’s no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg’s footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space. We shouldn’t ignore the fact many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it’s exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy – after all we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sport – but we should also recognise many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space. Unanswered questions remain If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are – to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for. A key final question is: what next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut. If the benefits are so tangible and important, we wouldn’t only do it once. articles.author: Nick Ames at the Etihad Stadium
articles.content: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Emirates Stadium
articles.content: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jen Sherman
articles.content: The US has more big chains but in Australia produce is better quality – and bread doesn’t taste like cake I poked. I pulled. I looked in confusion at the head of garlic I was holding, wondering why the cloves weren’t coming apart. When I dug my nails in and finally broke out a clove, its skin was pierced and there were scratch marks in the flesh. It had only been a few weeks since I moved back to Australia from the US, after a 10-year stint in San Diego; only a few weeks since I cooked with garlic cloves. Surely I hadn’t lost finger strength that quickly? Turns out, it wasn’t me. It was the garlic. Since that first Australian head of garlic, I’ve discovered that Australian garlic is tighter than the US variety. Over there, a few gentle rubs prise the cloves apart. Here, you’ve really got to put some effort in – I suspect that’s why you can buy a packet of garlic cloves in supermarkets and I never saw such a product in the States. Garlic in Australia is more expensive, too. Continue reading...

articles.content: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100th anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. If Sunday was Gary Neville’s Sistine Chapel [ Monday’s Football Daily ], then his commentary on the Fernando Torres goal for Chelsea against Barcelona must be his David ” – Ronnie McMahon. Regarding Declan Hackett’s assertion [ Monday’s letters ] that Donald Trump will be helping his mate Mauricio Pochettino by ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card, perhaps Poch should be careful what he wishes for: Trump may equally decide to get Michael Carrick reinstated, as he also has a bit of previous for that sort of thing” – Dexter O Riordan. In all the time that I have been watching football, I don’t think I have ever seen a player dismiss himself and be away down the tunnel before given a red card. Thanks James Tarkowski ” – Nigel Sanders. Brighton had only failed to win twice in the league since 5 September. A 1-1 draw with Leeds and a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool - their only opponents with double letters in their name. That bizarre hoodoo struck again at Hull on Sunday. Good good news for Seagulls fans is the only double-lettered encounters they have before hosting Hull in February are trips to Forest and Spurs. Even better news is that since that 1-1 draw with Leeds on 5 September, they have a 100% win record against sides without double letters and have not conceded a goal” – Dan Ashley (and no others). Chinese media have reacted with glee to the dramatic reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, with one commentary warning against future “witch-hunts”. An article published on Tuesday in the state-run outlet the Global Times said US media reports about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset were “malicious” and “negatively impacted American public perception of China”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.content: Users can give agents tasks such as booking travel or buying presents, but glitches have been reported Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to? Want to avoid the Christmas shopping hordes? Then let your AI agent do the shopping for you. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on your apps – and the high street. Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app stores, having been downloaded millions of times. However, UK regulators have said they are keeping a close eye on the launch over privacy and consumer protection requirements. Continue reading...

articles.author: Edward Helmore
articles.content: New York City mayor notes ‘massive impact’ on working Americans’ lives when Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO Zohran Mamdani , New York City ’s mayor, on Monday weighed in on the corporate turbulence surrounding Nvidia and the chipmaker’s chief executive officer, Jensen Huang , saying he does not think working Americans “signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of … Huang’s fidelity to his marriage”. The mayor said Huang “had a massive impact”, with Nvidia’s share price dropping dramatically when Huang stepped down as the company’s CEO on 12 November after a reported extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Continue reading...

articles.content: Australians also turn against AI datacentres, with nearly half saying they don’t want one near their home Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese’s approval ratings have nosedived in the latest Guardian Essential poll, with the prime minister reaching his highest level of disapproval after his net popularity plummeted 10 points in just a month. articles.content: Last week Australia’s second-largest retailer, Coles, reported it had been targeted in a cyber attack. It follows countless other hacking disruptions around the globe, from attacks on fridges across Europe and blood banks in France to multi-billion dollar cryptocurrency heists. With each event causing panic and disorder, experts and the public are left asking if we’re in the age of a new type of cyber warfare. Global technology editor Dan Milmo speaks to Reged Ahmad about what is being done to keep our systems safe and how vulnerable we all are to a new online danger Read more: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? articles.author: Donna Lu
articles.content: We are offered a seemingly endless array of drinks and foods that now come with the world’s most consumed psychoactive drug Read more in the Antiviral series Feeling tired and need a pick-me-up but finding your morning cup of coffee isn’t touching the sides? Instead of the predictable choice (a second coffee), you could instead opt for a seemingly endless array of other drinks and foods that now come with added caffeine. You might energise yourself before your morning gym session with a few caffeinated scoops of a pre-workout supplement. Afterwards, you could refuel with a caffeinated protein shake or a protein bar with added guarana – whose seeds contain caffeine. Continue reading...

articles.content: Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view. Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geostrategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Cordon
articles.content: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. Continue reading...

articles.author: Michael Hogan
articles.content: Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. The stale previous seasons are fast becoming a mere memory When Nigella Lawson helps crown the new champion of The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday night, two other winners will also be celebrating: the show itself and broadcaster Channel 4. The fabled “Nigella effect” has freshened up a franchise that was beginning to taste distinctly stale. Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence. Continue reading...
